notes.text: The ghosts you meet on the road in India | Condé Nast Traveller India Skip to main content The Latest Destinations Hotels & Homestays Food & Drink People & Culture BLACK BOOK Readers' Travel Awards Mindful Travel Video CNT TOP RESTAURANT AWARDS We had just turned left on NH17 at Khunia More in the heart of Chapramari Wildlife Sanctuary when, apropos nothing, I said: “These forests look so full of ghosts.” NJP Station, where Rajib, the driver, had picked us up in his Tata Sumo, was now two hours and some change back. The early winter darkness had formed clumps in the dense overgrowth by the bumpy road and was slowly clawing its way up to the tall tree canopy. And the lot I was travelling with—my parents, an aunt, two cousins, and Rajib—had gone silent, taking in the melancholic scenery. “Look for wild animals,” my father muttered, leaving “you moron” unsaid. He was always the naturalist and I the supernaturalist, which was one of the many things that disappointed him about me. “ Ghosts , did you say?” Rajib jumped in, rescuing me from any further admonitions. “Strange that you should say it at this very moment!” “That turn we left behind?” Rajib began narrating his tale. Rajib had just started working as a driver with an agency in Siliguri. And it was just his second or third trip on this route when he’d dropped someone off some ten-odd kilometres beyond Khunia More and was on his way back. It was nighttime, but the hour wasn’t very late when he crossed Khunia More. “This young man and woman hailed my car, asking for a lift. Now, we have a stringent policy of not taking passengers outside bus stops or scheduled pick-ups. So I drove past them. I’d just driven past them a few metres when I second-guessed myself and turned around. A stranded couple in the middle of this forest—I could certainly drop them some distance. Nobody would know. So I turned around. Not far ahead of the junction, just twenty, maybe thirty metres ahead. But when my headlights swept the spot, nobody was there! No vehicle had passed by me in the few seconds that I crossed them and had turned around. And there is nowhere other than this road to go. You can see the forest for yourselves—you can't just walk into it, can you? My hair at the back of my neck stood up, and I knew this wasn’t ok. I turned around and sped off to Siliguri.
